content: Hello, I would like to discuss the formalization of Numerical Analysis results using the new AI models. I am a PhD student in this field and I am new to lean. Based on my own experiments it seems quite easy to formalize theorems in lean with the new AI models. I have been starting with a very simple result, the discrete Gronwall lemma. In a semiring, if $u_{k + 1} \leq c_k u_k + b_k$ and $c_k \geq 0$ for $k = n_0, \ldots, n - 1$, then $u_n \leq u_{n_0} \prod_{i = n_0}^{n - 1} c_i + \sum_{k = n_0}^{n - 1} b_k \prod_{i = k + 1}^{n - 1} c_i$. I have generated the lean file with ChatGPT and I put it in Analysis/ODE with the name DiscreteGronwall.lean. Can I commit, push and open the PR for this?

It's very unlikely that a Lean beginner driving an AI can prepare a PR that Mathlib would accept at this point. (You are not the first to discover that LLMs can write Lean. :-)

I would love to have some experts get together and write a roadmap for Tau Ceti for numerical analysis, so we could start receiving AI-written PRs there. (See #Tau Ceti > Getting started: roadmaps.)
Thank you! I will ask people I know in the numerical analysis community if they are interested in creating a roadmap.
What kind of numerical analysis do you have in mind? Floats? Exact real numbers...?

I was thinking more of exact real numbers for now. Maybe a first goal could be time discretizations for ODEs, Galerkin methods or ((Quasi) Monte Carlo) quadrature. Maybe it makes sense in lean to first establish some abstract stability and error propagation results?

What would you like to do?

I would also be interested in formalizing some parts of Numerical Analysis. In the far future I would like to formalize some parts of Numerical Linear Algebra, but I think starting with some discretized methods would be better. I don't think that Galerkin methods or even Finite Difference methods exist in Mathlib. I agree that trying to abstract stability/consistency/convergence would be beneficial, but maybe we should not abstract too soon. Maybe after exploring some of discretization first and after figuring out how to abstract will be beneficial.

@Fabian Zehetgruber There were also some project porting https://github.com/rocq-community/math-classes/ and corn.
That might give a good start.

I have two open PRs (1, 2), proving convergence of the Euler Method for ODEs. I think Mathlib does not have a maintainer interested in developing numerical analysis at the moment, so it's tough to get NA in mathlib.
I don't think the maintainer response to heavily LLM generated PRs is indicative to their response to PRs in a given field in general, so I wouldn't be discouraged out of hand

Vasily Ilin said:

I think Mathlib does not have a maintainer interested in developing numerical analysis at the moment

4 different maintainers reviewed your PR...

4 different maintainers reviewed your PR...

I worked with each one to address all comments. The PR got stuck anyway though. I have asked around and was told that the main issue is that there is no maintainer interested in NA, not the fact that v1 of the PR was LLM-generated.

@Fabian Zehetgruber by the way, if you want to go heavy in the AI workflow, an alternative to Tau Ceti (perhaps even more interesting from a numerical analysis perspective!) is to pick your favourite not-too-complicated feature from numpy/scipy/etc, and try to see if you can get an implementation in lean working with floating point, say using https://github.com/lecopivo/NumLean. Then you can happily automate away all the proofs of correctness since they would not be the main point anyway (unlike in mathlib). Argbualy not unlike what @Kim Morrison has been doing with hex if I am not mistaken.
